Before anyone quotes equipment, answer six questions about the building itself. The answers decide whether unit metering is straightforward, complicated, or the wrong tool for now.
Who owns and reads the master meter?
If the utility owns it and bills the owner directly, you have a clean upstream figure to reconcile against each cycle.
What do local rules allow?
Some jurisdictions cap the charge and require itemized invoices. Confirm this before a design is drawn.
How many units, and how are they supplied?
Count suites, common areas and any shared branch. A building where four suites share one riser needs a different layout from one with a panel per suite.
Which services are worth metering?
Electricity and water are the usual starting points. Thermal and gas depend on whether heating and cooking are central or per unit.
How much of the bill sits in common areas?
That figure tells you how much cost stays with the owner once unit charges begin.
Who maintains the equipment afterwards?
Seals, calibration records, billing queries and replacements all continue long after commissioning day.

Then ask for a site review rather than a quote.   • How many units, and how are they supplied? Count suites, common areas and any shared branch. A building where four suites share one riser needs a different layout from one with a panel per suite.
  • Which services are worth metering? Electricity and water are the usual starting points. Thermal and gas depend on whether heating and cooking are central or per unit.
  • How much of the bill sits in common areas? That figure tells you how much cost stays with the owner once unit charges begin.
  • Who maintains the equipment afterwards? Seals, calibration records, billing queries and replacements all continue long after commissioning day.

Then ask for a site review rather than a quote. Axis Meter Solutions offers a free consultation with a submetering specialist about your property, with no obligation, and the scope runs from equipment selection and installation through tenant billing, maintenance and compliance planning, so you can see which parts your building needs.

Get the layout and the billing terms in writing before committing: which services are metered, who reads them, how common area consumption is allocated, how vacant units are treated, and how a disputed charge is resolved. A design that matches the building beats a design that matches a brochure.
